title: Trapped-ion quantum simulation of (1+1)D SU(2) lattice gauge theory via loop-string-hadron formulation
summary: We present a quantum simulation of the SU(2) lattice gauge theory in 1+1 dimensions with one flavor of fermions, performed using the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H2. This work is based on the loop-string-hadron (LSH) formulation of the gauge theory, and is distinguished by using qubits to represent both bosonic-gauge and fermionic-matter degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we access the $j=1$ electric-flux sector beyond the $j_{\max}=1/2$ truncation commonly used in SU(2) quantum simulations. To that end, we digitize an electric-field degree of freedom using a multiqubit register for representing the bosonic quantum number. Our simulation therefore synthesizes several key ingredients relevant to quantum simulations in higher spatial dimensions, in particular explicit local gauge-field degrees of freedom represented here by a multiqubit bosonic register, while relying solely on circuit-construction optimizations that are expected to scale polynomially with lattice size. This work demonstrates that modern quantum hardware is increasingly able to accommodate the features of complicated but physically important lattice gauge theories while successfully reproducing the expected Trotterized dynamics.

AI.tldr: Researchers have simulated the SU(2) lattice gauge theory in 1+1 dimensions with fermions using a trapped-ion quantum computer, incorporating both bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom, and extending to the j=1 electric-flux sector. They used a multiqubit register to represent the electric-field degree of freedom, showing that current quantum hardware can handle complex gauge theories with good scalability.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to demonstrate the capability of modern quantum hardware, specifically the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H2, to simulate more complex aspects of lattice gauge theories, such as including both bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom, and exploring beyond the commonly used $j_{\max}=1/2$ truncation to the $j=1$ electric-flux sector. This work aims to push the boundaries of what can be achieved with quantum simulations and to establish a path towards simulating higher-dimensional theories.
AI.method: The method involves using the loop-string-hadron (LSH) formulation of the gauge theory and employing qubits to represent both the gauge and matter fields. The researchers digitized the electric-field degree of freedom using a multiqubit register to access the $j=1$ electric-flux sector. They optimized the circuit construction for efficient scaling with the size of the lattice, which is crucial for future simulations in higher spatial dimensions.
AI.result: The result is a successful simulation of the SU(2) lattice gauge theory dynamics, with the expected Trotterized behavior, using a quantum computer. The study shows that it is feasible to include explicit local gauge-field degrees of freedom, represented by a multiqubit bosonic register, and to extend the simulation to a higher electric-flux sector, all while maintaining polynomial scaling with the lattice size. This suggests that the approach can be scaled up for more complex systems.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that current quantum computing technology, exemplified by the trapped-ion system, has reached a level where it can effectively simulate elements of physically important but intricate lattice gauge theories. The ability to incorporate multiqubit representations of bosonic registers and to explore beyond typical truncations opens the door to more advanced quantum simulations, particularly in higher dimensions, and demonstrates the potential for quantum computers to contribute to our understanding of fundamental physics.

title: One-loop mixing matrix of the N=1 SYM Supercurrent operator upon renormalization on the Lattice using stout-smeared Links
summary: We extend the perturbative investigation of the renormalization and mixing patterns of the supercurrent operator in lattice ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SYM) theory, using stout-smeared gauge links. We employ the SLiNC action for gluinos and a family of Symanzik improved gauge actions for gluons. Building upon previous studies employing clover-improved fermions and the Wilson gauge action, we compute the one-loop mixing matrix of the supercurrent operator among gauge-invariant and gauge-variant operators. Particular emphasis is placed on the structure of operator mixing in the presence of stout smearing parameters. Our results contribute toward refining fine-tuning strategies necessary for the restoration of supersymmetry in the continuum limit, and provide a stepping stone for future perturbative and nonperturbative investigations in supersymmetric theories on the lattice.

AI.tldr: The paper explores the renormalization and mixing of the supercurrent operator in ${\cal N}=1$ SYM theory on a lattice, using stout-smeared gauge links, SLiNC action for gluinos, and Symanzik improved actions for gluons. It presents one-loop mixing matrix results and discusses implications for supersymmetry restoration.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to refine the fine-tuning strategies needed for restoring supersymmetry in the continuum limit by examining the supercurrent operator's behavior under different lattice conditions, specifically with stout smearing, which was not as thoroughly investigated before.
AI.method: The method involves extending previous studies by incorporating stout-smeared gauge links, employing the SLiNC action for gluinos, and using a family of Symanzik improved gauge actions for gluons. The authors calculate the one-loop mixing matrix for the supercurrent operator, considering both gauge-invariant and gauge-variant operators.

This work contributes to the understanding of how to restore supersymmetry in lattice simulations.

title: Recent Advances in Transverse-Momentum--Dependent Distributions in Lattice QCD
comment: 63 pages, 15 figures. Invited review article; accepted for publication in Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics
summary: Unraveling the three-dimensional structure of hadrons is a central objective in modern nuclear and particle physics. Transverse Momentum Dependent parton distributions (TMDs) provide crucial insights into the interplay between partonic transverse motion and spin, and are indispensable for describing a wide range of high-energy processes at facilities such as JLab, COMPASS, the LHC, and the upcoming Electron-Ion Collider. In recent years, significant progress has been made in accessing TMDs from lattice QCD using novel approaches. Methods based on ratios of Mellin moments, large-momentum effective theory (LaMET), and Coulomb-gauge techniques have enabled first-principles investigations of the Collins-Soper kernel, intrinsic soft functions, TMD wave functions, and TMDPDFs. Recent lattice results for both unpolarized and spin-dependent distributions, including the Boer-Mulders function, demonstrate the feasibility of extracting transverse-momentum--dependent information directly from QCD. This paper reviews recent advances in lattice-QCD studies of TMDs, outlines remaining challenges such as continuum and infinite-momentum extrapolations, and discusses future directions toward precision determinations of hadron structure in three dimensions.

It also addresses the challenges and future prospects for more precise determinations.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide an overview of the advancements in using TMDs to understand the 3D structure of hadrons, which is crucial for explaining high-energy processes at various experimental facilities. The paper aims to highlight the novel approaches in lattice QCD that have enabled the study of TMDs, as well as the remaining challenges and future directions in this field.

These approaches have been used to investigate the Collins-Soper kernel, intrinsic soft functions, TMD wave functions, and TMDPDFs, leading to the extraction of transverse-momentum-dependent information from QCD.

This has provided valuable insights into the interplay between partonic transverse motion and spin, contributing to our understanding of hadron structure in three dimensions.

The paper calls for continued research to achieve more accurate and comprehensive determinations of the 3D structure of hadrons.

title: Expansion schemes for finite density QCD equation of state: which one is the best?
summary: The finite density equation of state of QCD is a fundamental quantity for understanding the phase structure of the theory, and also for the realistic modeling of the QCD medium in simulations. While direct lattice simulations at finite density are extremely challenging, several expansion schemes have been devised to extrapolate into the QCD phase diagram. All of these schemes are based on susceptibilities of conserved charges, i.e. derivatives of the pressure with respect to the chemical potential(s). In this work we set out to determine which of these schemes possesses the best convergence properties. To this end, we employ extreme-statistics lattice simulations on a $16^3\times8$ lattice, which allow us to obtain susceptibilities up to order eight with remarkably small errors. We compare in particular two methods, based on contours of constant (normalized) baryon density and of constant entropy density. We find that the latter converges more quickly, effectively requiring susceptibilities only up to order four to cover the chemical potential range up to at least $μ_B \approx 500$ MeV. We also extend the comparison to the three dimensional space of chemical potentials, and find that the entropy-based method consistently shows superior convergence.

AI.tldr: This paper compares different expansion schemes for determining the finite density equation of state in QCD, using lattice simulations. It finds that a method based on constant entropy density shows better convergence properties than one based on constant baryon density, requiring only up to 4th order susceptibilities to cover a significant range of chemical potentials.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to identify the most efficient and accurate method among the existing expansion schemes for extrapolating into the QCD phase diagram, which is crucial for understanding the theory's phase structure and for realistic modeling of the QCD medium in simulations.
AI.method: The authors use extreme-statistics lattice simulations on a $16^3\times8$ lattice to obtain high-order (up to 8th) susceptibilities with small errors. They compare two methods: one based on contours of constant (normalized) baryon density and another based on constant entropy density. The comparison is extended to the three-dimensional space of chemical potentials to evaluate the convergence of each method.
AI.result: The results show that the method based on constant entropy density has superior convergence properties, needing only up to 4th order susceptibilities to accurately describe the QCD medium for chemical potential values up to approximately 500 MeV. This finding holds true even when the analysis is expanded to the three-dimensional space of chemical potentials.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that for the purpose of extrapolating the QCD equation of state to finite density, the expansion scheme based on constant entropy density is more efficient and provides a better description of the system, as it converges faster compared to the method based on constant baryon density.
